# A Short History of Railway Signalling

## Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- describe why railway signalling developed as railways became faster and busier;
- explain the relationship between signals, points, block working and interlocking;
- recognise the main stages from hand signals to computer-based signalling;
- relate historical practice to the equipment and principles used by modern S&T staff;
- explain why signalling history is still useful when fault finding or reading older documentation.

## Why this matters

Railway signalling is sometimes taught as a collection of separate subjects: signals, points, train detection, interlocking, level crossings, power supplies and control systems. In practice, these subjects grew together. Each stage in the history of signalling was a response to a real operating problem: how to keep trains apart, how to route them safely, how to communicate with drivers, and how to make sure that a single human error did not become a disaster. Often innovations and changes to rules and methods came about due to accidents, and the same can be said for the railway in general. Almost every rule is "written in blood." Some knowledge of the history is therefore useful to understand the importance of why things we do today are necessary.

A background knowledge of the history also helps to demystify some of the modern terminology. Knowing the history explains why many terms sound mechanical even when the equipment is electronic. We still talk about locking, levers, routes, blocks, clearing a signal, proving a point and replacing a signal to danger. These words come from earlier methods of working with levers and semaphore signals, but the ideas behind them are still present all the way through relay based interlockings, to solid state interlockings and computer-based control centres.

This chapter gives a broad overview of the history, with later chapters going into more technical detail of the individual systems.

## The problem signalling had to solve

The basic problems of railways is simple:

> A train cannot steer or stop quickly.

::: callout-tip
## Trivia

The contact patch between each train wheel and the rail is approximately the same as a 10p coin. There is very little friction between the wheels and the rail, which goes some way to explaining why the stopping distances are so great.
:::

Once a train is moving, the driver cannot steer around an obstruction. The route must be set and known to be clear before the train arrives, and there must be enough distance to stop if the route is not safe. Signalling exists to control these conditions.

Early railways were slower, less frequent and often worked by simple local arrangements. On some lines, a railway employee might give a hand signal, display a flag, or use a lamp at night. These methods were easy to understand, but they depended heavily on local knowledge, good visibility and disciplined working. In the very early days, trains were divided by time, with a train not allowed to follow until a set time had passed. This was safe, providing the first train did not break down, and the second train was not faster than the first...

As railways expanded, three problems became more urgent:

- trains needed to follow one another without catching up;
- trains needed to pass through junctions without conflicting moves;
- drivers needed clear instructions at a distance, in all weather and at different times of day.

Modern signalling can be seen as the engineering answer to those problems.

::: {.callout-note title="Think about it"}
Imagine a single track railway with one train in each direction. If there is no place to pass and neither driver can see the whole line ahead, what information must be known before either train is allowed to enter the section?
:::

## Hand signals, flags and lamps

The earliest form of railway signalling was direct human communication. A person near the line could use hand signals, coloured flags or lamps to tell a driver whether to proceed, stop, or approach cautiously. These people were initially policemen, hence why signallers are still occasionally referred to as "bobbies". The limitation with using hand signals was that the signal was only reliable as the person displaying it, and was not particularly visible in poor weather and with the limited view available to the driver in steam trains. Fog, darkness, curves, cuttings, and lineside buildings could all make a signal harder to see.

These limitations did not make hand signalling useless. Even today, handsignalling, flags and lamps have a place in possession work, degraded working and emergency arrangements. These circumstances are carefully controlled, and are generally only used for slow speed movements.

::: callout-important
## Important

One important handsignal to remember is the emergency stop, where two hands are raised above the head. In darkness a red lamp can be used, or any light waved vigorously.
:::

## Fixed signals

The next important step was the fixed signal. Instead of relying only on a person standing at the lineside with a flag or lamp, railways installed equipment at fixed locations to give drivers consistent instructions.

There were a variety of early signals used, but mechanical semaphore signals became the common solution. A semaphore arm could be held horizontal to show that it was not safe to proceed and raised or lowered to show that the line ahead was clear. At night, coloured spectacle lenses and a lamp gave a corresponding indication. The exact appearance and meaning varied between railway companies, but the general principle was the same.

Fixed signals brought several advantages:

- the signal was always in the same place so the driver could learn where to expect it;
- the signal could be placed higher to improve visibility;
- the signal could be worked from a safer or more convenient location;
- the signal could be connected mechanically to other equipment.

That last point was crucial for the development of more sophisticated systems. Once signals and points could be worked by levers, rods, wires and pulleys, it became possible to link their operation together. This led to the development of interlocking.

## Points, routes and conflicting movements

Points allow a train to move from one line to another. They are essential for junctions, loops, sidings and yards, but they introduce risk. If points are not set correctly, a train can be sent in the wrong direction. If points move under a train or are not closed fully, the train can derail. If two trains are sent over conflicting routes then a crash is inevitable.

To make sure that the route ahead of a train is safe all the points in the route must be fully closed, correctly set, and any conflicting route must be prevented.

This is the idea behind interlocking. In its simplest form, interlocking ensures that the equipment can only be operated in a safe sequence. For example:

- a signal cannot be cleared unless the relevant points are correctly set;
- points cannot be moved while a signal reading over them is cleared;
- two signals cannot be cleared at the same time if their routes conflict.

The word "interlocking" comes from mechanical locking between levers. In a traditional lever frame, each lever worked a signal, point or lock. Mechanical tappets and locking bars prevented unsafe combinations. The signaller did not have to rely only on memory; the equipment physically resisted an unsafe movement as the mechanical bars were "interlocked" to prevent them moving out of sequence.

::: {.callout-tip title="Technician's link"}
When you later study relay interlocking or computer-based interlocking, keep this mechanical idea in mind. The technology has changed, but the purpose is recognisably the same: prove that the route is safe before authority is given to the driver.
:::

## The signal box

The signal box brought local control together in one place. From the signal box, a signaller could operate points and signals using a lever frame, observe trains, communicate with neighbouring boxes and keep a record of train movements.

Many features of signalling practice grew around the signal box:

- lever numbers and signal box diagrams;
- bell codes and block instruments for communication between boxes;
- train registers (a log book of all the movements made);
- local instructions for special layouts;
- mechanical detection to allow remote working of signals and points.

The signal box also created a clear division of responsibility. The driver obeyed the signals. The signaller set routes and controlled the section. The S&T staff maintained the equipment that made the system dependable.

This division is still visible today, although the physical workplace may now be a signalling centre rather than a lineside box.

## Time interval and absolute block

One of the earliest ways of separating trains was time interval working. A train would be allowed to follow another train after a specified time had passed. This was better than having no rule at all, but it had an obvious weakness: if the first train stopped unexpectedly, time alone did not prove that the line ahead was clear.

Block working developed to solve this problem. The railway was divided into sections, and the aim was to prevent more than one train being in a block section at the same time. On double track railways, this principle allowed trains to follow one another in the same direction while maintaining a controlled separation.

Absolute block working became a major method of operation. Adjacent signal boxes communicated with each other, traditionally using bell codes and block instruments. Before accepting a train, the box in advance had to confirm that the line was clear according to the rules of that system.

This allowed a change in the mindset from having to assume that a train has gone because enough time had passed, to being able to prove that the train had passed through the section and that therefore the line **must** now be clear. It was common to refer to a train having passed "complete with tail lamp" as unless the red light on the rear of the train was spotted by the next signal box there was always the possibility that the train had split in two and left some carriages behind. Signalling moved to having to establish that a section of railway was clear before being able to allow another train to enter it.

## The telegraph and communication

The electric telegraph transformed railway operation because it allowed information to travel faster than the train. Signal boxes could communicate with each other over distance, and control of trains became less dependent on sight alone. Before telephones all communication between signal boxes was done via telegraphs, and to this day mechanical signal boxes still use bell-codes as the primary method of communication. Although they will now have a telephone to the next signal box, the actual signalling of trains is still done via the official bell-codes.

This is a good reminder that railway signalling did not develop in isolation. It used available technologies from other fields and adapted them to railway safety, although at times somewhat slower than other industries. Mechanical engineering provided levers, rods and locks. Electrical engineering provided telegraph circuits, instruments, relays, track circuits and later electronic systems. Computing provided data-driven interlocking, control systems and automatic route setting.

## Track circuits and train detection

Block working originally depended on people and procedures to establish whether a section was clear. Train detection introduced a further engineering safeguard: a method of directly detecting whether a train was within a section, or more importantly that a section is clear.

In a basic track circuit, the rails form part of an electrical circuit. When a train's wheels and axles occupy the section, they provide a path between the rails and change the state of the circuit. This allows the signalling system to detect that the line is occupied. Due to its fail-safe nature a track circuit is best thought of as *proving the absence of a train* as they are designed to fail in such a way that they will give an occupied indication (there are some exceptions to this, and these must be treated as serious failures).

Track circuits made several developments possible:

- continuous proof that a section was clear or occupied;
- automatic replacement of signals to danger after a train passed;
- automatic signalling on busy lines;
- electrical interlocking controls based on train position.

## Colour light signals and electric operation

Semaphore signals were effective, but they had limitations. They required moving mechanical parts at the signal, mechanical transmission from the signal box, and lamps for night indications. As electrical technology became more reliable, railways increasingly adopted colour light signals. Electric lights provided better reliability and better visibility. As technology progressed many colour light signals now use LED lights rather than filaments, which are brighter and more reliable yet.

Colour light signals use coloured aspects to instruct the driver. Multi-aspect signalling allows a driver to receive advance information about the state of the route ahead. For example, a sequence of aspects can warn the driver to expect a stop signal and brake in good time. This allows the frequency of trains to be increased.

Electric operation also changed points. Mechanical point operation by rods and cranks was suitable for many layouts, but distance, complexity and required operating force limited the practical maximum distance. Power-operated points allowed larger areas to be controlled from a single location and reduced the amount of physical effort required by the signallers to move them. Proving that the point had completed its movement and was now fully closed in the other position now became possible electrically too.

## Relay interlockings

Relays allowed interlocking logic to be built electrically. Instead of using only mechanical locking in a lever frame, circuits could prove conditions and energise relays when those conditions were satisfied.

Relay interlockings could handle larger and more complex layouts than purely mechanical systems, and required less space and maintenance. They also supported remote control, panel signal boxes and route setting. A signaller could press buttons or operate switches to request a route, while the relay circuits checked that the necessary conditions were met.

The basic questions remained familiar:

- Are the required points detected in the correct position?
- Is the track clear?
- Are conflicting routes normal or locked?
- Is the overlap available?
- Is the approach locking condition satisfied?
- Can the signal show a proceed aspect?

::: {.callout-note title="In practice"}
When fault finding on a relay interlocking it's often useful to work backwards. For example, if a signal will not clear, the question is not simply "What is broken?" but "Which required condition has not been proved?"
:::

## Automatic warning and train protection

As train speeds increased, it became more important to support the driver beyond the visual signal alone. A driver may miss a signal, misread an aspect, or be unable to brake sufficiently if warning is inadequate.

Automatic Warning System (AWS) introduced a standard in-cab warning linked to the state of the signal or warning equipment on the approach. Train Protection and Warning System (TPWS) was later introduced to reduce the risk from signals passed at danger and overspeed at selected locations.

These systems do not replace signalling. They add layers of defence. The main signalling system controls the movement authority; warning and protection systems help manage the risk that the authority is misunderstood, missed or exceeded.

This layered approach is a recurring theme in railway safety. No single measure is treated as perfect. Rules, equipment, design, maintenance, training and human factors all contribute.

## Solid state and computer-based signalling

From the late twentieth century onwards, signalling increasingly moved from relay logic to electronic and computer-based systems. Solid State Interlocking (SSI) and later computer-based interlockings use data and software to implement the interlocking rules. Rather than a large room of relays the same operations and logic can be performed by just a few computer cubicles.

This has dramatically changed fault-finding. Instead of tracing circuits, checking contacts, and measuring voltages the process is much similar, with often one faulty module simply swapped out for another under the guidance of a Box TO checking the computer terminal, however the underlying principles coded into the interlocking are no less complex:

- the route ahead still needs to be proved clear;
- points still need to be commanded, moved, detected and locked;
- signals still need to display the correct authority;
- conflicting routes still need to be prevented;
- failures still need to move the system towards a safer state.

The change is only where the logic takes place. In a mechanical interlocking it is done with chucks of metal physically blocking each other. In a relay interlocking many switches and circuits are used. In a computer-based interlocking it is lines of code.

## Control centres and traffic management

Many older signal boxes controlled a relatively small local area. Modern signalling centres can control large areas, sometimes covering routes that previously required many boxes. This has changed the signaller's interface with the railway.

Control systems may include:

- signaller workstations;
- route-setting systems;
- train describers;
- automatic route setting;
- timetable and traffic management tools;
- voice and data communications;
- remote condition monitoring.

For technicians, this widens the system boundary. A fault report may involve lineside equipment, a location case, a relay room, a transmission link, a workstation display, a data configuration issue, or an interface between systems. Historical knowledge helps because it gives you the stable principles underneath the changing technology.

## From lineside signals to cab signalling

Traditional signalling gives authority through lineside signals. The driver observes the signal and responds to its aspect. On higher-speed or high-capacity railways, lineside signals may become limiting. The driver may need information earlier, more continuously, or in a form better suited to the train's speed and braking performance.

Cab signalling and systems such as the European Train Control System (ETCS) move more information into the driving cab. Depending on the application, the system can supervise movement authority, speed and braking curves. This does not remove the need for signalling principles. It changes how those principles are communicated and enforced.

A useful way to think about the progression is:

- early signalling: a person gives an instruction locally;
- fixed signalling: equipment gives a visible instruction at a known place;
- block and interlocking: the instruction is controlled by rules and locked equipment;
- train detection: the railway proves where trains are;
- train protection: the system intervenes if limits are exceeded;
- cab signalling: movement authority is displayed and supervised in the train.

Each stage adds capability, but each stage also depends on the earlier safety questions.

## Why older systems remain in use

Railways keep equipment in service for a long time. This is not simply because replacement is expensive, although cost and access are important. It is also because signalling equipment is safety-critical and deeply connected to the physical railway.

Replacing a signalling system can affect:

- track layouts and point machines;
- cable routes and location cases;
- power supplies;
- level crossings;
- telecoms and data links;
- operating rules and training;
- rolling stock interfaces;
- maintenance competence and spare parts.

For that reason, a technician may encounter equipment from several generations during the same career, or even on the same route. A modern workstation may control a relay interlocking. A computer-based interlocking may interface with conventional track circuits. A power-operated point may still be understood using principles that began with mechanical locking.

::: {.callout-warning title="Avoid a common mistake"}
Do not assume that newer equipment changes the safety principle. A diagnostic screen may replace a row of relays as the technician's first view of the fault, but the railway still needs the same proofs before it can safely authorise a movement.
:::

## Worked example: a signal will not clear

Consider a simple junction where a train is to be signalled from a main line into a loop. The signaller requests the route, but the signal remains at danger.

A historical way of thinking through the problem is useful:

1.  The hand-signalling question: is it safe to tell the driver to proceed?
2.  The fixed-signal question: is the signal able to display the correct instruction?
3.  The points question: are the points set for the loop?
4.  The interlocking question: are conflicting routes prevented?
5.  The block question: is the line ahead available?
6.  The train-detection question: is the route and overlap clear?
7.  The proving question: has the equipment actually proved those conditions?

In a mechanical signal box, some of these answers would be found through lever positions, locks and block instruments. In a relay interlocking, they may be found through relay states and circuit diagrams. In a computer-based interlocking, they may be found through indications, diagnostic messages and event logs.

The technology changes the method of investigation, but the reasoning pattern is continuous.

## Activity

Look at the following list and place the items in a likely historical order:

- computer-based interlocking
- hand signal
- relay interlocking
- semaphore signal
- track circuit
- cab signalling
- absolute block

Then, for each item, write one sentence explaining what problem it helped to solve.

::: {.callout-note title="Guidance"}
Do not worry about exact dates for this activity. The aim is to connect each development with an operating need. For example, a track circuit helped the railway detect whether a section of line was occupied.
:::

## Key points

- Railway signalling developed because trains needed reliable control over distance, speed, routing and separation.
- Fixed signals made instructions more consistent than hand signals alone.
- Block working controls the separation of trains by dividing the railway into sections.
- Interlocking prevents unsafe combinations of signals, points and routes.
- Track circuits and other train detection systems provide direct evidence of train position.
- Relay, solid state and computer-based systems use different technology to apply many of the same safety principles.
- Historical knowledge helps technicians understand modern terminology, diagrams and fault-finding logic.

## Check your understanding

1.  Why was time interval working weaker than block working?
2.  What is the basic purpose of interlocking?
3.  Why must point position be proved rather than merely commanded?
4.  How did track circuits change the way signalling systems could detect trains?
5.  Give one example of a signalling term that comes from older technology but is still used today.
